title: 05. Load Balancing & Scalability: NGINX
summary: NGINX is an open-source web server, reverse proxy, and Layer 4/7 load balancer built around an event-driven, single-threaded-per-worker architecture that achieves tens of thousands of concurrent connections per process with…
objectives: Why is NGINX's event-driven architecture able to handle 10K+ concurrent connections where Apache's prefork model struggles?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** NGINX is an open-source web server, reverse proxy, and Layer 4/7 load balancer built around an event-driven, single-threaded-per-worker architecture that achieves tens of thousands of concurrent connections per process with predictable memory and CPU usage.

NGINX was created in 2002 by Igor Sysoev specifically to solve the "C10K problem" — how to handle 10,000 concurrent connections on a single server, which Apache's then-dominant prefork model could not. Apache prefork used one process per connection, so 10,000 connections meant 10,000 processes, each consuming 2-8 MB of memory — clearly unsustainable. NGINX's design choice was radical: a small number of worker processes (typically equal to the CPU core count), each running a single-threaded event loop that uses `epoll` (Linux) or `kqueue` (BSD) to handle thousands of connections concurrently via non-blocking I/O. A connection that's waiting on the backend doesn't block the worker — the worker registers it with `epoll`, moves to the next ready connection, and is notified by the kernel when the backend responds. The result is that 10,000 idle connections consume ~10,000 file descriptors plus a few KB of memory each (say 100 MB total), versus Apache's 20-80 GB. This is why NGINX powers some of the highest-traffic sites on Earth: Netflix, Instagram, Dropbox, GitHub, WordPress.com — all run NGINX at the edge.

The **configuration-driven** model is NGINX's signature. Behavior is declared in a hierarchical config: `http` block contains `server` blocks (virtual hosts), each containing `location` blocks (URL patterns), each containing directives (`proxy_pass`, `rewrite`, `return`). NGINX parses this config at startup (or on `nginx -s reload`), compiles location regexes, builds a routing tree, and serves requests by walking the tree. The advantage is operational: a single text file (`/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`) describes the entire edge behavior, can be version-controlled in Git, and is reviewed in pull requests. The disadvantage is that the config syntax is idiosyncratic (braces, semicolons, context-sensitive directives) and small mistakes cause silent misbehavior (a missing semicolon can route traffic to the wrong upstream). Tools like `nginx -t` validate syntax before reload, but semantic errors (e.g., a `location` block that catches more than intended) require testing in staging.

NGINX supports **both Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and Layer 7 (HTTP) load balancing**. The `stream` block does L4 — it proxies raw TCP/UDP based on destination port, useful for databases (PostgreSQL on 5432), Redis (6379), or proprietary binary protocols. The `http` block does L7 — it parses HTTP, can read headers, cookies, URL paths, and route based on any of them (`location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api_backend; }`). Most production deployments use L7 for HTTP traffic (because you can do path-based routing, header manipulation, SSL termination) and L4 only for non-HTTP protocols. NGINX Plus (the commercial version) adds active health checks, session persistence, and dynamic upstream reconfiguration; the open-source version relies on passive health checks (marking a backend down after failures observed in real traffic) and requires config reload to change upstream pools. The `nginx-upstream-dynamic-servers` and `ngx_http_dyups_module` third-party modules add dynamic upstream control to open-source NGINX, and the commercial `ngx_http_api_module` exposes a REST API for upstream management.

**SSL termination** is one of NGINX's core use cases. NGINX terminates the client's TLS connection (presents a certificate, performs the handshake, decrypts incoming bytes), then proxies the request to the backend over plain HTTP (or re-encrypted HTTPS). This offloads cryptographic work from the application servers (which can focus on business logic), centralizes certificate management at the edge, and enables HTTP-level features (path routing, header injection) on the decrypted traffic. NGINX's TLS implementation uses OpenSSL, supports TLS 1.3 (1-RTT handshake, vs TLS 1.2's 2-RTT), and can serve thousands of certificates via SNI (Server Name Indication) — `ssl_certificate` and `ssl_certificate_key` directives per `server` block, with the correct cert selected based on the `Host` header / SNI in the ClientHello. **HTTP/2** is enabled with a single directive (`listen 443 ssl http2;`) and gives multiplexing (multiple requests over one TCP connection), header compression (HPACK), and server push — significantly reducing latency for modern web apps. **HTTP/3 over QUIC** is supported via the `nginx-quic` build (mainline since 1.25.0), bringing 0-RTT connection setup and immunity to TCP head-of-line blocking.

The **event loop** is the engineering core. Each worker process enters a loop: call `epoll_wait` to get a list of ready file descriptors (sockets with data to read, sockets ready to write, errors); for each ready FD, run the appropriate handler (accept a new connection, read the request, proxy to upstream, write the response); loop forever. The loop is non-blocking — every I/O call is async (set the socket to non-blocking, register with `epoll`, return immediately). If a worker takes too long on one connection (e.g., a slow backend), other connections in that worker queue up — this is why NGINX defaults to multiple workers (one per CPU core) and uses techniques like `worker_connections 10240` (each worker handles up to 10K concurrent connections) and `multi_accept on` (a worker accepts all pending connections at once per `epoll` wake-up). Real-world benchmarks: a single NGINX worker on a modern CPU can sustain 50,000+ HTTP requests/second for static files (no upstream), and 5,000-20,000 req/s for proxied requests (bottlenecked by upstream response time). Netflix's edge NGINX fleet handles millions of concurrent connections per region.

**Lua scripting** (via the `ngx_http_lua_module` / OpenResty distribution) extends NGINX beyond static config into a programmable edge. Lua code runs inside the NGINX worker (via LuaJIT, a fast Lua compiler), can access request data (headers, body, cookies), call upstreams, manipulate the response, and even run sub-requests — all without leaving the worker process. Cloudflare, Kong, and OpenResty-based API gateways build their entire edge logic on this — they handle rate-limiting, request rewriting, JWT validation, and traffic shaping in Lua, without ever hitting the backend. The advantage is performance (Lua runs in-process, no IPC overhead); the disadvantage is complexity (debugging Lua inside NGINX requires the `error_log` and a deep understanding of NGINX's request lifecycle phases). For most teams, plain NGINX config plus a separate API gateway (Envoy, Kong, Linkerd) is simpler than embedding business logic in NGINX via Lua.

The trade-offs versus HAProxy and Envoy are nuanced. NGINX is the **swiss army knife** — it does web serving, reverse proxy, LB, SSL termination, caching, and HTTP/2 in one binary, with the most mature ecosystem. **HAProxy** is more focused: it's purely a LB/proxy (no static file serving), with better stats, more sophisticated load-balancing algorithms (dynamic weighted RR, least-connections with slow-start), and a long reputation for bulletproof reliability in high-throughput L4 scenarios. **Envoy** (from Lyft/CNCF) is the modern successor: dynamic configuration via xDS APIs (no reloads), deep observability (every request traced), and first-class support for service mesh (Istio, Consul Connect). For a startup or mid-size team: NGINX is the default; for a high-throughput L4 LB in front of databases: HAProxy; for a service mesh or dynamic cloud-native deployment: Envoy. Netflix uses NGINX at the edge for SSL termination and HTTP routing, and an internal Zuul-based gateway for application-level concerns; Instagram uses NGINX for the same edge role plus heavy use of OpenResty for request rewriting.

(each worker handles (non-blocking) (non-blocking) 10K+ concurrent conns) WORKER EVENT LOOP (one iteration): epoll_wait() -> [fd5: read-ready, fd8: write-ready, fd12: read-ready] | +-- fd5 (client socket): read HTTP request bytes | parse headers, match location block | if /api/* -> proxy_pass to upstream "api_backend" | open upstream socket fd20, set non-blocking | register fd20 with epoll for write-ready | +-- fd8 (upstream socket, was waiting to write): | write request to backend | re-register fd8 for read-ready (wait for response) | +-- fd12 (upstream socket, response arrived): read response, write to client fd5 if request complete: close or keep-alive fd5 (no blocking syscalls - every I/O is async via epoll) +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ | Client |----->| NGINX |----->| Backend | | TLS |<-----| SSL term|<-----| HTTP | +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ (one worker handles 10K such conns) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The master process reads `nginx.conf`, binds listening ports (80, 443), and forks one worker process per CPU core. Each worker enters an event loop that calls `epoll_wait` to receive notifications about ready file descriptors (client sockets with incoming data, upstream sockets with responses, new connections on the listening socket). 2. When a client connects, one worker's `epoll_wait` returns the listening socket as read-ready; the worker calls `accept()`, gets a new socket FD, sets it to non-blocking, registers it with `epoll`, and continues. Subsequent client data triggers `epoll_wait` again, the worker reads the HTTP request, parses headers, matches a `location` block, and decides whether to serve a file, return a redirect, or `proxy_pass` to an upstream. 3. For proxied requests, the worker opens a non-blocking socket to the chosen upstream backend (round-robin by default; `least_conn` and `ip_hash` are alternatives), registers it with `epoll`, writes the request, and continues serving other clients while waiting. When the upstream responds, `epoll_wait` notifies the worker, which reads the response and writes it back to the client. No worker blocks; thousands of concurrent connections share the same worker.

quiz.explanation: Apache prefork uses one process per connection, so 10,000 concurrent connections require 10,000 processes. Each process has its own address space, stacks, and interpreter state — typically 2-8 MB of RSS per process, so 10K connections means 20-80 GB of RAM just for connection state, plus the OS overhead of context-switching between 10K processes on each I/O.

quiz.explanation: The http block does Layer 7 load balancing: NGINX parses HTTP requests (method, URL, headers, body), can route based on URL path (location /api/), manipulate headers, terminate SSL, serve cached responses, and so on. Backends see a normal HTTP request — NGINX adds X-Forwarded-For, Host, etc. The stream block does Layer 4: NGINX proxies raw TCP/UDP bytes without parsing the application protocol.

quiz.question: How does NGINX do zero-downtime config reload, and what are the gotchas?
options: 100% CPU on NGINX workers usually means the event loop is busy doing CPU-bound work, not just I/O.

quiz.explanation: nginx -s reload (or kill -HUP ) triggers a reload. The master receives SIGHUP, re-parses the config, and if valid, forks new worker processes with the new config. It then sends SIGTERM to the old workers — but the old workers don't die immediately; they stop accepting new connections and finish in-flight requests, then exit gracefully (default 60-second timeout, after which they're force-killed).
